power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

info.title: Personality Prediction from Moments to Lifetimes

author.affiliation:
Davis, Psychology Department
								University of California

Davis, Psychology Department
								University of California

Department of Medical Social Sciences
								Northwestern University Feinberg School of Medicine

Department of Medical Social Sciences
								Northwestern University Feinberg School of Medicine

text.text: Personality is robustly linked to long-term outcomes, yet predicting momentary behavior (i.e., who does what, when, and where) remains challenging.

We argue that personality and its outcomes can be understood at multiple levels within an emergent hierarchy, and that prediction requires identifying what level(s) is most informative for a given target.
Broad traits reliably predict distal outcomes such as cognitive aging and mortality but reveal little about underlying processes.
Within-person patterns capture shorter-term regularities, though heterogeneity is often overlooked.
Momentary processes unfold as complex, multivariate systems that support personalized prediction but challenge generalization.
We therefore propose a bottom-up integrative framework that derives comparable features from person-specific dynamics and tests whether they predict outcomes at other levels.
Emerging evidence suggests that such features can bridge levels and support more integrative, explainable prediction.
Personality is a strong predictor of major life outcomes, including longevity, health, wealth, relationship quality, and occupational success (e.g., Ozer & Benet-Martínez, 2006).
text.formatted: Personality is a strong predictor of major life outcomes, including longevity, health, wealth, relationship quality, and occupational success (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">Ozer & Benet-Martínez, 2006</ref>).

text.text: Yet links between personality and specific behaviors remain elusive (e.g., Beck & Jackson, 2022b).
text.formatted: Yet links between personality and specific behaviors remain elusive (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">Beck & Jackson, 2022b)</ref>.

text.text: This challenge, raised decades ago by Jerry Wiggins (Wiggins, 1973), stems from assumptions that broad traits should predict narrow behaviors across time and from debates over whether narrow predictors are required for narrow outcomes.
text.formatted: This challenge, raised decades ago by Jerry Wiggins <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">(Wiggins, 1973)</ref>, stems from assumptions that broad traits should predict narrow behaviors across time and from debates over whether narrow predictors are required for narrow outcomes.

text.text: We propose that accurate personality prediction depends on aligning the representation of personality to the outcome being predicted.
A single level may be sufficient for some prediction questions, whereas others may require spanning levels and require their integration i .
Personality can be represented at many nested levels of organization and timescale in an emergent hierarchy (Beck et al., 2026; see the first column of Figure 1).
text.formatted: Personality can be represented at many nested levels of organization and timescale in an emergent hierarchy <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(Beck et al., 2026</ref>; see the first column of Figure <ref type="figure">1</ref>).

text.text: We focus on three representations commonly studied in personality psychology: Broad dispositions that summarize between-person differences, within-person patterns that characterize regularities across occasions or contexts, and momentary states and processes.
We refer to these as macro-, meso-, and micro-level representations, respectively, while recognizing that their placement is relational rather than absolute.

When applied, clearly delineating levels of personality constructs and outcomes can improve prediction of short-and long-term outcomes and support scalable interventions and policy development (Bleidorn et al., 2019).
text.formatted: When applied, clearly delineating levels of personality constructs and outcomes can improve prediction of short-and long-term outcomes and support scalable interventions and policy development <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(Bleidorn et al., 2019)</ref>.

text.text: Figure 1.
text.formatted: Figure <ref type="figure">1</ref>.

text.text: Linking an emergent hierarchy of personality to its implications for predictions.

The first column depicts the theoretical model: Momentary states and processes contribute to personlevel organization and population-level regularities through bottom-up emergence, whereas higher-order structures constrain the range, probability, and stability of lower-level dynamics.
The second and third columns show common personality representations and prediction targets at relatively macro-, meso-, and micro-levels.
Levels are relational rather than fixed, and higherorder regularities are not assumed to be simple aggregates of lower-level processes.
The paper proceeds as follows: We first provide a brief background on personality as an emergent hierarchy and its implications for personality prediction across levels.

Next, we review theory and evidence at each level, highlighting personality prediction and health as running examples drawn from our research program, and conclude with a generative research paradigm aimed at bridging levels.
We argue that understanding personality prediction requires first understanding what personality is and what is retained or obscured by different operationalizations.
Our prior work connects operationalizations of personality by conceptualizing personality as a nonlinear dynamic system embedded in an emergent hierarchy (Beck et al., 2026; see Figure 1).
text.formatted: Our prior work connects operationalizations of personality by conceptualizing personality as a nonlinear dynamic system embedded in an emergent hierarchy <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(Beck et al., 2026</ref>; see Figure <ref type="figure">1</ref>).

text.text: From this perspective, higher-order regularities emerge from the organization of lower-level processes and, in turn, constrain the range, probability, and stability of those processes.
Causal influence is therefore distributed across levels, making simple mechanistic causes unlikely to reside within any single construct or level (Hoel, 2026).
text.formatted: Causal influence is therefore distributed across levels, making simple mechanistic causes unlikely to reside within any single construct or level <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">(Hoel, 2026)</ref>.

text.text: Consequently, prediction and explanation are related but separable goals.
Broad dispositions can summarize regularities across people that predict consequential distal outcomes without constituting the mechanisms that generate them.
Because causes and predictive information are distributed across levels, no level is intrinsically privileged.

Each operationalization -broad population-level summaries, recurring within-person regularities, and dynamics of momentary processes -therefore contains different information whose predictive utility must be evaluated relative to the focal prediction problem.
In the next section, we illustrate this for broad, macro-level traits and outcomes.
Personality traits summarize broad between-person differences in thinking, feeling, and behaving.

From the perspective of an emergent hierarchy, the recurrence of a Big Few likely reflects shared biological, social, and environmental constraints that channel behavior into similar population-level regularities without implying a common causal architecture across persons (Beck et al., 2026).
text.formatted: From the perspective of an emergent hierarchy, the recurrence of a Big Few likely reflects shared biological, social, and environmental constraints that channel behavior into similar population-level regularities without implying a common causal architecture across persons <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(Beck et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: Despite this, broad traits still predict consequential distal outcomes because they summarize consequential patterns across time and context, even when they do not reveal the unique pathways through which those outcomes arise within a person.

Because health and mortality reflect the accumulation of behavior and exposure over long periods, they provide especially revealing tests of whether and which broad traits identify people at risk for chronic disease, cognitive decline, and earlier death (Beck & Jackson, 2022a).
text.formatted: Because health and mortality reflect the accumulation of behavior and exposure over long periods, they provide especially revealing tests of whether and which broad traits identify people at risk for chronic disease, cognitive decline, and earlier death <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(Beck & Jackson, 2022a)</ref>.

text.text: Findings consistently show that high conscientiousness and low neuroticism protect against chronic conditions, mortality, and cognitive decline, suggesting personality traits can serve as an early risk marker.

For example, conscientiousness and neuroticism robustly predict dementia diagnoses across eight international samples (Beck et al., 2024), and increases in neuroticism also predict dementia (Yoneda et al., 2020).
text.formatted: For example, conscientiousness and neuroticism robustly predict dementia diagnoses across eight international samples <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(Beck et al., 2024)</ref>, and increases in neuroticism also predict dementia <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">(Yoneda et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: However, several challenges remain due to complex cross-level connections.
First, personality-health associations are not always consistent across the lifespan; for instance, positive conscientiousness-health associations weaken with age (Luo et al., 2023).
text.formatted: First, personality-health associations are not always consistent across the lifespan; for instance, positive conscientiousness-health associations weaken with age <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">(Luo et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Second, personality appears more useful for understanding responses to biological burden than predicting burden itself.

Studies aiming to link traits with neuropathology rarely find direct links (Beck et al., 2024), yet traits predict cognitive resilience (better cognitive function despite pathology) with higher conscientiousness and lower neuroticism linked to greater resilience (Graham et al., 2021).
text.formatted: Studies aiming to link traits with neuropathology rarely find direct links <ref type="bibr">(Beck et al., 2024)</ref>, yet traits predict cognitive resilience (better cognitive function despite pathology) with higher conscientiousness and lower neuroticism linked to greater resilience <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">(Graham et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: Finally, trait-outcome associations may reflect reverse causality (e.g., poor health increasing negative emotions).

Yet, outcomes like mortality offer a clearer directional test; decades of findings consistently link higher neuroticism to early mortality and conscientiousness, and to a lesser degree openness and extraversion, to longer survival.
These effects remain after adjusting for demographics and replicate worldwide (Graham et al., 2017; Jokela et al., 2013; Willroth et al., 2025).
text.formatted: These effects remain after adjusting for demographics and replicate worldwide <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">(Graham et al., 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">Jokela et al., 2013;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">Willroth et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Combined with inconsistent evidence that long-term outcomes shape personality (e.g., Bleidorn et al., 2018), this work suggests personality traits are more influential than the reverse.
text.formatted: Combined with inconsistent evidence that long-term outcomes shape personality (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">Bleidorn et al., 2018)</ref>, this work suggests personality traits are more influential than the reverse.

text.text: Macro-level research links efficient, economical trait measures to consequential outcomes, offering practical value for identifying broad health risks.
Yet, like the therapist's dilemma, these associations identify who is at risk more readily than why, often requiring mesoand micro-level accounts for intervention (Levine et al., 1992).
text.formatted: Yet, like the therapist's dilemma, these associations identify who is at risk more readily than why, often requiring mesoand micro-level accounts for intervention <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">(Levine et al., 1992)</ref>.

text.text: Relative to broad dispositions, the meso level focuses on recurring patterns in behavior and experience across occasions or contexts.

Theoretically, accumulated behavior is assumed to (1) link traits to long-term outcomes (Ozer & Benet-Martínez, 2006); (2) link states to traits (Fleeson & Jayawickreme, 2025); and (3) drive personality change (Wrzus & Roberts, 2017).
text.formatted: Theoretically, accumulated behavior is assumed to (1) link traits to long-term outcomes <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">(Ozer & Benet-Martínez, 2006)</ref>; (2) link states to traits <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">(Fleeson & Jayawickreme, 2025)</ref>; and (3) drive personality change <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">(Wrzus & Roberts, 2017)</ref>.

text.text: Empirically, repeated assessments distinguish between-person differences from within-person associations over time (i.e. the ecological fallacy), which may differ in direction, while also revealing heterogeneity in those within-person associations.
Thus, people with similar trait levels may still exhibit different recurring patterns linking personality states to consequential behaviors and experiences.
Even similar recurring behaviors may reflect different underlying processes.

For example, agreeable behavior may arise from responsiveness to others' needs for one person but from an instrumental desire for approval or cooperation for another, with different implications for downstream outcomes.
Yet meso-level personality prediction remains limited.
First, much research straddles macro and meso levels by asking who engages in meso-level behaviors rather than when.

For instance, traits predict health care utilization (HCU): Higher conscientiousness, extraversion, and openness and lower neuroticism are linked to preventive HCU, whereas lower conscientiousness and agreeableness and higher neuroticism predict hospitalization risk (Atherton et al., 2024; Weston et al., 2024; Willroth et al., 2023).
text.formatted: For instance, traits predict health care utilization (HCU): Higher conscientiousness, extraversion, and openness and lower neuroticism are linked to preventive HCU, whereas lower conscientiousness and agreeableness and higher neuroticism predict hospitalization risk <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(Atherton et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">Weston et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">Willroth et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Such findings clarify who uses care but not the conditions under which they do so.

Our work with middle-aged and older adults further illustrates this gap: Higher trait conscientiousness predicts poorer average working memory, yet moments of higher conscientiousness predict better working memory (Ma et al., 2026), indicating that macro-level findings can misguide meso-level intervention.
text.formatted: Our work with middle-aged and older adults further illustrates this gap: Higher trait conscientiousness predicts poorer average working memory, yet moments of higher conscientiousness predict better working memory <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">(Ma et al., 2026)</ref>, indicating that macro-level findings can misguide meso-level intervention.

text.text: Second, particularly in health research, longitudinal studies often rely on long timescales (years or decades) that do not match the processes of interest (Hopwood et al., 2022).
text.formatted: Second, particularly in health research, longitudinal studies often rely on long timescales (years or decades) that do not match the processes of interest <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">(Hopwood et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: For example, people report better health in years they are less neurotic and more extraverted and conscientious than usual (Luo et al., 2022), yet shorter-term fluctuations (e.g., daily), which may distinguish individuals with similar trait levels, are more rarely investigated.
text.formatted: For example, people report better health in years they are less neurotic and more extraverted and conscientious than usual <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">(Luo et al., 2022</ref>), yet shorter-term fluctuations (e.g., daily), which may distinguish individuals with similar trait levels, are more rarely investigated.

text.text: The rise of intensive longitudinal data (e.g., ecological momentary assessment) has enabled prediction in daily life; for instance, moments of higher conscientiousness and lower extraversion predict better momentary cognitive performance (Ma et al., 2026), highlighting actionable timescales for intervention.
text.formatted: The rise of intensive longitudinal data (e.g., ecological momentary assessment) has enabled prediction in daily life; for instance, moments of higher conscientiousness and lower extraversion predict better momentary cognitive performance <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">(Ma et al., 2026)</ref>, highlighting actionable timescales for intervention.

text.text: Third, within-person studies reveal substantial individual differences in when and for whom personality states predict health behaviors, yet this heterogeneity is rarely treated as a central object of inquiry.

Because predictors of between-person variation are less often examined, it remains unclear whether individuals showing certain within-person patterns simply differ due to psychosocial or demographic factors.

Although recent work has examined between-person moderators of within-person associations (i.e., cross-level interactions), this literature has focused primarily on demographic rather than personality moderators, pointing to an important direction for future research.

The meso level captures recurring organization across occasions and models both withinperson associations and heterogeneity in them, yielding more specific intervention targets than broad traits alone.
However, common models limit examination of multiple interacting processes.
The next section considers how micro-level systems approaches may help bridge levels.
While personality traits show robust links to meso-and macro-level outcomes, accurately predicting momentary outcomes (i.e. what someone will do in a given moment) remains elusive.

Effect sizes for predicting short-term behaviors and long-term events are relatively small, in part because outcomes are multiply determined (Götz et al., 2022) and traditional methods are poorly suited to modeling that complexity.
text.formatted: Effect sizes for predicting short-term behaviors and long-term events are relatively small, in part because outcomes are multiply determined <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">(Götz et al., 2022)</ref> and traditional methods are poorly suited to modeling that complexity.

text.text: Advances in intensive longitudinal assessment, machine learning, and dynamic-systems theory are enabling progress in forecasting whether and when individuals enact specific behaviors (Beck & Jackson, 2022b).
text.formatted: Advances in intensive longitudinal assessment, machine learning, and dynamic-systems theory are enabling progress in forecasting whether and when individuals enact specific behaviors <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Beck & Jackson, 2022b)</ref>.

text.text: At the micro level, systems approaches operationalize personality within persons as multivariate configurations of affective, cognitive, and goal processes unfolding over time and context (Beck et al., 2026; Beck & Jackson, 2020b).
text.formatted: At the micro level, systems approaches operationalize personality within persons as multivariate configurations of affective, cognitive, and goal processes unfolding over time and context <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(Beck et al., 2026;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">Beck & Jackson, 2020b)</ref>.

text.text: This person-specific focus allows the processes predicting behavior to differ across individuals and models transactions among psychological processes and environments (Beck & Jackson, 2020a; Lee & Beck, 2025; Nissen & Beck, 2025b).

text.text: Whole Trait Theory similarly links broad traits to state distributions; we treat those distributions as one possible intermediate representation rather than the privileged explanation or endpoint of personality prediction (e.g., Fleeson & Jayawickreme, 2025).

text.text: Research on personality dynamics and intensive longitudinal research are too broad to review fully here.

We therefore focus on how person-specific systems approaches can improve momentary prediction; the following section considers how features derived from these systems may inform prediction at other levels.
A long-standing question in behavior prediction concerns the relative importance of person versus situation factors (Mischel, 1968).
text.formatted: A long-standing question in behavior prediction concerns the relative importance of person versus situation factors <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">(Mischel, 1968)</ref>.

text.text: Although both show similar effect sizes across studies, evidence for person × situation interactions (i.e. individuals with certain traits responding differently to context) remains sparse (Kuper et al., 2024).
text.formatted: Although both show similar effect sizes across studies, evidence for person × situation interactions (i.e. individuals with certain traits responding differently to context) remains sparse <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">(Kuper et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Rather than asking which factor "wins" on average, the crucial question is when and for whom each matters (Beck & Jackson, 2022b).
text.formatted: Rather than asking which factor "wins" on average, the crucial question is when and for whom each matters <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Beck & Jackson, 2022b)</ref>.

text.text: Answering that question requires multivariate models that allow both the relevant predictors and their importance to vary across people. Beck and Jackson (2022b) used person-specific machine learning to determine whether person factors, situation factors, or their combination best predicted subsequent behavior.

text.text: As illustrated in Figure 2, the same behavior arose from different antecedent structures across individuals.
text.formatted: As illustrated in Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">2</ref>, the same behavior arose from different antecedent structures across individuals.

text.text: Prediction depended on ensembles of both person and situation factors for some people, primarily situation factors for others, primarily person factors for others, and a single feature of either the person or situation for still others.
Such heterogeneity was not simply across people but also occurred within individuals across behaviors.

Across seven subsequent behaviors and experiences, prediction accuracy exceeded chance, but individuals differed in both prediction strength and the features most important for predicting their behavior.

These findings suggest that modest historical success in momentary behavior prediction may reflect models that impose common, low-dimensional explanations on behavior generated by heterogeneous and multivariate processes.

Micro-level prediction therefore benefits from models that preserve person-specific configurations of person and situation information rather than assuming that the same predictors operate similarly across people.
behavior prediction.
However, person-specific models do not readily reveal how these dynamics relate to recurring patterns or broader traits and outcomes.
The next section considers integrative prediction across levels.
Given the near-infinite combinations of potential antecedents, a common critique is that a person-specific systems approach lacks utility because it does not generalize across people.

Within an emergent hierarchy, however, generalization need not require identical lower-level processes across individuals or assume that those processes must reproduce existing higher-level trait structures.

We argue that the more promising path is bottom-up discovery: Model personspecific dynamics, derive comparable features of those systems, identify regularities across heterogeneous individuals, and test whether those regularities are stable and consequential.

As illustrated in Figure 3, this approach begins with person-specific dynamics and tests which system features recur across individuals, remain stable over time, and predict outcomes at other levels, rather than selecting lower-level dynamics because they resemble existing trait summaries.
text.formatted: As illustrated in Figure <ref type="figure">3</ref>, this approach begins with person-specific dynamics and tests which system features recur across individuals, remain stable over time, and predict outcomes at other levels, rather than selecting lower-level dynamics because they resemble existing trait summaries.

text.text: A roadmap for bottom-up integration and its links to personality prediction.
The roadmap begins by modeling heterogeneous, person-specific systems from dense longitudinal data (bottom), then extracting comparable features that capture their organization and dynamics.

These features are evaluated for recurrence across people, stability or systematic change over time, and associations with meaningful outcomes before being translated into scalable assessment, prediction, and intervention.
Network, dynamical, and structural features illustrate possible implementations rather than required methods.
This proposal yields clear empirical tests.

System features should show meaningful regularities across individuals despite heterogeneity, demonstrate stability or systematic change over time, and predict meso-or macro-level outcomes, ideally beyond broad trait measures.
If they do not recur, behave coherently over time, or improve prediction, they offer little value for connecting levels.
Network and differential-equation models, which we briefly review below, provide two possible ways to estimate such features rather than necessary components of the broader framework.
Prior work represented person-specific systems of Big Five states as N=1 time-series networks and found evidence that these representations were longitudinally stable (Beck & Jackson, 2020a , 2021).
text.formatted: Prior work represented person-specific systems of Big Five states as N=1 time-series networks and found evidence that these representations were longitudinally stable <ref type="bibr">(Beck & Jackson, 2020a</ref> <ref type="bibr">, 2021)</ref>.

text.text: Building on this, Nissen and colleagues tested whether features of network organization predicted long-term personality trait change (Nissen & Beck, 2025a) and distal outcomes (Nissen et al., 2026).
text.formatted: Building on this, Nissen and colleagues tested whether features of network organization predicted long-term personality trait change <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">(Nissen & Beck, 2025a)</ref> and distal outcomes <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">(Nissen et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: These features were largely unrelated to changes in selfreported traits but predicted changes in informant-reported traits and several distal outcomes.

For example, systems that more closely resembled a Big Five structure predicted socially desirable trait changes and several positive distal life outcomes, indicating that people with socially desirable trait structures may be rewarded for being better able to navigate social norms.

Differential-equation models provide a complementary approach by estimating personspecific features such as attractor location (a set point or "home base") and strength (how strongly someone is pulled back toward that home base).

In positive and negative emotion systems -core components of personality systems -these features have shown concurrent and prospective associations with depressive symptoms and life satisfaction, as well as longitudinal stability (Long et al., 2026; Springstein et al., 2026).
text.formatted: In positive and negative emotion systems -core components of personality systems -these features have shown concurrent and prospective associations with depressive symptoms and life satisfaction, as well as longitudinal stability <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">(Long et al., 2026;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">Springstein et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: Together, these studies illustrate how features derived from heterogeneous person-specific systems can be evaluated as meaningful individual differences without judging them by whether they reproduce familiar trait dimensions.
Integrative prediction connects heterogeneous person-specific processes to broader outcomes through comparable system features.
Its value depends on whether those features are stable, comparable across people, and predict outcomes beyond simpler summaries.
We conclude by considering how this framework can guide prediction across levels.
We distinguished three levels of personality prediction and outlined opportunities for bottom-up integration.
Although we focused on health, the framework also applies to several other domains like mental health and relationships (Long et al., 2026).
text.formatted: Although we focused on health, the framework also applies to several other domains like mental health and relationships <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">(Long et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: No level is inherently more useful or fully distinct.
Because personality is an emergent hierarchy, causal contributions may occur across scales, making the most informative representation an empirical question (Hoel, 2026).
text.formatted: Because personality is an emergent hierarchy, causal contributions may occur across scales, making the most informative representation an empirical question <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">(Hoel, 2026)</ref>.

text.text: That broad traits predict outcomes so consistently is notable, but their utility differs from lower-level representations: Broad dispositions may identify risk, within-person patterns may reveal how it is expressed, and momentary processes may guide individualized tailoring.
Integrating heterogeneous micro-level processes with meso-and macro-level representations may yield more flexible, explainable predictions of who is at risk, what a person may do, and when (Table 1).
text.formatted: Integrating heterogeneous micro-level processes with meso-and macro-level representations may yield more flexible, explainable predictions of who is at risk, what a person may do, and when (Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_0">1</ref>).

text.text: Such integration may move psychology closer to describing, predicting, and explaining what people think, feel, and do.

Leverage multi-modal and multi-timescale data, such as passive sensing (e.g., actigraphy), environmental data (e.g., pollution), EMA, etc.
Pair EMA and repeated cognitive tasks with passive measures of sleep and activity across measurement bursts.
Apply methods that capture complex dynamic associations across multiple timescales, such as differential equations.
Estimate which momentary factors predict cognitive performance for each person and identify recurring vulnerabilities, such as social isolation and poor sleep quality.
Model change in within-person patterns and momentary dynamics from measurement burst designs and assess their convergence with broader assessments.
Test whether person-specific predictors remain stable across bursts and whether changes correspond to longerterm cognitive functioning.
Compare broadly targeted interventions with approaches tailored to each person's dominant predictor (e.g., sleep, stress, or positive affect).
